pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11; how climate change is affecting the poles — Arctic sea ice is shrinking fast (its September minimum is falling about 12–13% per decade), the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are losing mass and raising sea level, permafrost is thawing and releasing methane (a powerful greenhouse gas), and these changes drive positive FEEDBACK LOOPS where melting causes more warming which causes more melting.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y6 links to human impact/environment; KS3 Chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' (greenhouse gases, human impact on climate) and KS3 Biology (human effects on ecosystems).
• Standards—US: NGSS MS-ESS3-5 (factors causing rise in global temperatures) and MS-ESS2-6/MS-ESS3-3 (human impact; climate system); 5-ESS3-1 earlier.
• Operational details: the central, hardest idea is the positive feedback LOOP. Teach two flagship loops: (1) ice-albedo — bright ice reflects sunlight; melt exposes dark ocean/land that absorbs more heat, warming and melting more; (2) permafrost-carbon — thaw releases methane/CO2, adding greenhouse warming that thaws more permafrost. Distinguish sea-ice loss (floating, doesn't itself raise sea level) from land-ice loss (raises sea level). Poles warm faster than the global average (polar amplification). Keep it evidence-based and cause-and-effect, not doom.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (9) state that the poles are warming and ice is shrinking; Tier B (10) explain one feedback loop (dark water/land absorbs more heat than bright ice); Tier C (11) distinguish sea-ice from land-ice effects on sea level and explain how a feedback loop accelerates change.
bestPractices: Teach the feedback loop as a CYCLE the pupil can trace round (melt → darker surface → more heat absorbed → more melt), not a one-off effect
Explicitly separate floating sea ice (melting doesn't raise sea level) from land ice sheets (melting does) to fix a stubborn confusion
Use real, current data (sea-ice extent graphs) so the trend is evidenced, not asserted
Name polar amplification — the poles warm faster than the global average — and connect it to the feedbacks
Keep an agency framing (causes are human emissions; outcomes depend on choices) rather than fatalism
keyRepresentations: Ice-albedo loop diagram: bright ice reflects → melt → dark ocean absorbs → warmer → more melt
Permafrost-carbon loop: thaw → methane/CO2 released → more warming → more thaw
Arctic September sea-ice extent graph showing the downward trend
Split diagram: floating sea ice (no sea-level change) vs land ice (raises sea level)
commonMisconceptions: Melting Arctic sea ice raises sea level — floating ice melting barely changes it; land ice (Greenland/Antarctica) is what raises seas
The poles warm at the same rate as everywhere else — they warm faster (polar amplification)
A feedback loop is a single effect — it is a self-reinforcing cycle where the output feeds back to grow the cause
Permafrost is just frozen soil with no climate role — thawing it releases methane/CO2 that add further warming
It's too late / nothing affects it — the pace depends on human greenhouse-gas emissions and choices

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: how climate change affects the poles, centred on the hardest idea — positive feedback LOOPS. Learners trace two self-reinforcing cycles (ice-albedo and permafrost-carbon), distinguish floating sea ice (melting barely changes sea level) from land ice sheets (melting raises sea level), and connect these to polar amplification (the Arctic is warming much faster than the global average; warming across Antarctica is more uneven). The headline interactive proposal has learners operate a climate dashboard so the self-feeding nature of a loop becomes causal and visible; supporting activities build the loop via ordering/sorting, a scientist-style spoken explanation, and evidence reading from real sea-ice data. Framing stays evidence-based and cause-and-effect, with agency (human emissions and choices affect the pace) rather than doom.

activities.title: Run the polar climate dashboard (operate the feedback loop)
feedback: If the learner expects melting to stop the instant they stop touching the control: draw attention to the curl-back arrow — 'the dark water you exposed is now absorbing extra heat and melting more ice; that is the loop feeding itself, making the change bigger than your nudge alone.'

If the learner thinks melting the floating sea ice raised the sea level: point to the almost-unmoved floating-ice gauge versus the clearly rising land-ice gauge, and name that floating ice already displaces its own weight of water (Archimedes), so its melting barely changes sea level.
Reinforce the 'cut emissions' observation: the pace depends on human choices, not fate.
activities.rationale: Feedback loops are made concrete by operating them: letting the melt continue after the learner stops acting shows the self-amplifying dynamic, and parallel gauges make the sea-ice vs land-ice distinction visible. The live gauges, curl-back arrow, and emissions lever are interaction examples, not required technology; a paper loop or demonstration could serve the same end.
sourceClaims: The poles warm faster than the global average (polar amplification); ice-albedo and permafrost-carbon feedbacks accelerate polar warming; land-ice loss (not floating sea ice) raises sea level
learnerActions: Nudge a temperature control up one notch and watch a patch of bright sea ice melt into dark open ocean
Watch an albedo (reflectiveness) meter drop and an 'absorbed sunlight' reading rise as bright ice becomes dark water

Stop touching the control and observe that the exposed dark water keeps absorbing extra heat and melts some more ice — an arrow curls back to show melt causing more melt, so the total change ends up bigger than your single nudge alone would cause
Open a second panel: thaw permafrost, watch methane/CO2 puff out, push the temperature up, and thaw still more permafrost
Compare two gauges: melting the FLOATING sea ice barely moves the sea-level bar, but tipping meltwater off the Greenland LAND ice sheet clearly raises it
Pull a 'cut emissions' lever and see every loop slow down
activities.intendedInsight: A positive feedback loop is a self-reinforcing cycle: the output (melted ice / released methane) feeds back to strengthen its own cause, so a warming push leads to more warming and melting than it would on its own. Only land ice adds significant water to the sea; floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water, so its melting barely changes sea level.

activities.title: Build the loop from parts (label and order the cycle)
feedback: If the learner leaves the stages as a straight line: ask 'where does the last step — warming increases — lead?' and have them draw the return arrow from 'warming increases' back to 'ice melts', showing the cycle feeds itself rather than ending.

If the learner sorts a floating sea-ice statement into 'raises sea level': remind them floating ice already displaces its own weight (Archimedes), so only land-ice melt (Greenland/Antarctic sheets) adds water to the sea.

A correct sort or ordering shows the learner can recognise and arrange the loop structure; follow it by asking them to explain in their own words why the loop accelerates, since the sort alone does not elicit that explanation.
activities.rationale: Ordering and sorting let learners construct the loop structure and practise the sea-ice/land-ice distinction; these help build and check understanding but on their own test recognition rather than eliciting a full independent explanation.
learnerActions: Lay out the stages of the ice-albedo loop — bright ice reflects sunlight; ice melts; dark ocean is exposed; more heat is absorbed; warming increases — and arrange them into a closed circle rather than a straight line
Draw the return arrow from 'warming increases' back to 'ice melts' to show the cycle feeds itself
Repeat for the permafrost-carbon loop: thaw → methane/CO2 released → more warming → more thaw
Sort statements into 'raises sea level' (land-ice melt) and 'barely changes sea level' (floating sea-ice melt)
activities.intendedInsight: Assembling the cycle shows that the final step loops back to the first, which is what distinguishes a feedback loop from a one-off change.

activities.title: Explain it like a climate scientist
feedback: If the learner lists facts without closing the loop ('dark water absorbs heat, ice is shrinking, permafrost thaws'): ask them to connect each step to the next and back to the start.

For the 'stayed white' question: if the surface stayed bright and kept reflecting sunlight, the extra absorbed-heat step disappears, so the ice-albedo loop would no longer amplify the melting — some melting would still happen from greenhouse warming, but less. This shows albedo is what drives this particular loop.
If the learner says 'it's too late': redirect to the emissions idea — the pace depends on human greenhouse-gas choices.
activities.rationale: A scientist-style spoken explanation with responsive follow-ups probes the causal reasoning directly. Explanation and operating the loop address different aspects, so this complements rather than replaces the dashboard.
learnerActions: In your own words, explain to a listener why Arctic sea ice loss is bigger than warming alone would cause — say what happens AND why the loop makes the change bigger
Add permafrost thaw as a second reinforcing loop in your explanation
Answer a probing follow-up: 'Is there anything that would make it slow down on its own, or does the loop only push one way?'
Answer: 'What if the ocean under the ice had somehow stayed white — would the melting still speed up?' and justify your answer
activities.intendedInsight: Producing a spoken cause-and-effect explanation forces the learner to close the causal circle and transfer the loop idea to a new case, rather than listing facts.

activities.title: Read the evidence: sea-ice extent over time
feedback: If the learner points only to one dip: highlight the multi-decade downward slope beneath the year-to-year variation.
Anchor the figure: the September minimum is declining about 12–13% per decade relative to the 1981–2010 average over the satellite record (the verified NASA value is ~12.2%).
activities.rationale: Using real current data keeps the claim evidence-based. Reading an actual graph and selecting the trend builds the habit of grounding conclusions in measurement.
sourceClaims: Arctic sea ice September minimum extent is declining at about 12.2% per decade relative to the 1981–2010 average, measured over the satellite record since 1979
learnerActions: Study an Arctic September sea-ice extent graph covering the satellite record (since 1979) and describe the trend in your own words
State roughly how fast the September minimum is falling per decade and explain how you read it from the graph
Answer: 'What's your evidence that the ice is really shrinking, not just moving around from year to year?'
activities.intendedInsight: The downward trend is evidenced by measured data, not asserted; a long record distinguishes a real decline from year-to-year wobble.

constraints: Teach the feedback loop as a CYCLE the learner can trace round (melt → darker surface → more heat absorbed → more melt), not a one-off effect.
Explicitly separate floating sea ice (melting barely changes sea level) from land ice sheets (melting raises sea level); justify with displacement (floating ice already displaces its own weight).
Name polar amplification (the Arctic is warming much faster than the global average; Antarctic warming is more uneven) and connect it to the feedbacks.
Keep an agency framing — causes are human emissions and outcomes depend on choices — rather than fatalism.

Ordering/sorting checks and the sea-ice-vs-land-ice sort mainly confirm and help build the loop structure; they do not by themselves elicit a full independent explanation, so pair them with a spoken or written explanation task.

The dashboard interaction examples (albedo meter, curl-back arrow, sea-level gauges, emissions lever) are illustrative mechanisms to make the loop visible; they are not mandatory, and paper loop diagrams, demonstrations, or graphs can serve the same objectives.
Use the ~12–13% per decade figure for the satellite record relative to the 1981–2010 average; present it as measured data, not a prediction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Only one source (NASA Arctic sea-ice minimum, ~12.2% per decade) is marked verified; the curriculum-standard and polar-amplification/feedback claims are marked unverified in the source row. Treat the ~13% headline and polar-amplification statements as legacy claims, not independently confirmed here.
The description/objective uses '13% per decade' while the verified NASA claim states ~12.2%; retained learner-facing as '~12–13%' to span both without asserting a precise figure.

Original artefact notes contained universal-superiority phrasing ('a static image can't convey the runaway dynamic', '3D adds nothing', dialogue 'better traced by operating it'); these were rescoped to narrow affordances. A fixed diagram can still teach the loop's parts; a live model additionally shows the self-amplifying dynamic — neither is claimed universally necessary.
'Floating ice melting barely changes sea level' is the accurate statement (tiny salinity/density effects exist); kept as 'barely changes' rather than 'does not change' for precision at this age.

sourceClaims were re-checked verbatim against the original sources[].claim strings; only sources[0] and sources[3] directly support the activities they are attached to, and both are copied exactly (including the en-dash in '1981–2010'). No source was treated as evidence of empirical effectiveness or of any medium's superiority.

probeDeeper: You've told me melting makes more melting. Is there anything that would make it slow back down on its own, or does the loop only push one way?
Permafrost is frozen ground holding trapped methane and CO2. If it thaws, how could that join the same kind of loop?
What's your evidence that the ice is really shrinking, not just moving around from year to year?
What if the ocean under the ice had somehow stayed white — would the melting still speed up?
assess.correctAnswer: Bright white ice reflects most of the Sun's energy back to space; dark ocean absorbs it. When ice melts it uncovers dark water, which warms up and absorbs more heat, which melts more ice, which uncovers more dark water — a self-reinforcing feedback loop, so the warming and melting accelerate rather than staying steady. (Arctic September sea-ice is declining about 12% per decade.)

errorPatterns.pattern: melting is a one-off, steady change — 'it just melts a bit more each year because it's a bit warmer', with no loop
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw the loop as a circle (less ice -> darker surface -> more heat absorbed -> less ice) and contrast with a straight line
errorPatterns.distractor: The air just gets a little warmer each year, so a little more melts each year
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes linear/steady melting with no self-reinforcement

errorPatterns.pattern: melting sea ice raises sea level — confuses floating sea ice with land ice ('all that melting ice is what floods cities')
errorPatterns.nextMove: floating ice already displaces its own weight (Archimedes); only LAND ice (Greenland/Antarctic sheets) adds to the sea
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes sea-level rise to Arctic sea-ice melt

errorPatterns.pattern: the poles are remote bystanders — 'it's far away, it doesn't affect us'
errorPatterns.nextMove: link to albedo and ocean circulation and global sea level; the poles are a climate engine
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats polar change as local and irrelevant

responseLevels.gap: Says the ice is melting 'because it's hot' with no mechanism, or claims melting sea ice floods the land.
responseLevels.full: Explains a positive feedback loop (less ice -> darker surface -> more absorbed heat -> more melting), can add permafrost/methane as a second reinforcing loop, distinguishes sea-ice (floating) from land-ice (sea-level) effects, and transfers the loop idea to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Names bits — dark water absorbs heat, ice is shrinking, permafrost thaws — but lists them without closing the loop; can't explain why the rate accelerates.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In summer the sea ice near the North Pole melts, showing dark ocean underneath. The next summer, even more ice melts than the year before. Why does the melting speed up year after year instead of staying the same? Tell me what's happening, and then tell me WHY that makes it get faster.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child without the feedback idea treats melting as a one-off, steady 'it's just a bit warmer' process; the feedback child explains the LOOP — melting causes conditions that cause more melting. The reason-tier forces the causal circle, not just 'the Earth is warming'.
